hops.title: Bacteria that carry electrons through centimeters of mud
hops.text: In a typical mitochondrial protein, a run of several electron hops spans about ten nanometers in all. On the muddy seafloor, cable bacteria carry electrons across a centimeter or more, roughly a million times farther. Identified in Denmark in 2012, each is a long chain of cells standing upright in mud. Deep down there is sulfide but no oxygen; at the top there is oxygen. Cells at the bottom strip electrons from sulfide and send them up conductive protein fibers in the shared cell envelope to cells near the surface, which hand them to oxygen. Those fibers conduct about as well as highly doped synthetic conducting polymers.

sources.citation: Pfeffer C, Larsen S, Song J, et al. Filamentous bacteria transport electrons over centimetre distances. Nature. 2012;491:218-221.
van der Veen JR, Hidalgo Martinez S, Wieland A, et al. ACS Nano. 2024;18(47):32878-32889.

hops.title: The oxygen you breathe in is made into water
hops.text: Ask a roommate where the oxygen you breathe in goes, and many will say it leaves as carbon dioxide. Not directly. That CO₂ comes from breaking down food. The O₂ your cells use goes to Complex IV, picks up electrons and protons, and becomes water. In 1949, two mice and a rat given heavy oxygen to breathe showed it in their body water, and some reached their exhaled CO₂ by swapping atoms with that water. At rest you make about 250 to 350 milliliters of metabolic water a day, mostly this way. Kangaroo rats, which almost never drink, get about half a gram of water per gram of dry seeds.

sources.citation: Dienel GA, Lauritzen M. Fluids Barriers CNS. 2025;22(1):44.

hops.afterHeading: Two machines that keep each other in step
hops.title: How a World War I munitions chemical became a 1930s diet drug
hops.text: During World War I, French factories used 2,4-dinitrophenol, DNP, to make munitions. In 1933, Maurice Tainter at Stanford reported that the same chemical raised people's metabolic rate and caused rapid weight loss, and it was soon sold over the counter without a prescription. The reason is this section's uncoupler. DNP lets protons leak back across the inner membrane, so the chain races, fuel burns faster, less of its energy is captured as ATP, and more leaves as heat. Nothing regulated that leak. People developed cataracts, and some died of overheating. After 1938, when a new federal law required drugs to be shown safe before sale, doctors stopped prescribing it.

sources.citation: Grundlingh J, Dargan PI, El-Zanfaly M, Wood DM. 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP): a weight loss agent with significant acute toxicity and risk of death. J Med Toxicol. 2011;7(3):205-212.
U.S. Food and Drug Administration. A brief history of the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research.

audio.title: A snow-melting flower, a cyanide-eating lemur and a vitamin surprise
audio.transcript:
In this lesson, the chain runs by the book: a pair of electrons from N A D H pushes out ten protons, a pair from F A D H two pushes out six, and the oxygen at the end becomes water. Living things add some surprising twists: electrons that take another route, a chain that meets a poison every day, and oxidants that act as messages. Here are three true stories.

First, walk through a wetland in eastern North America in late winter, and you might find a purple-hooded flower sitting in a neat hole it has melted in the snow. That is eastern skunk cabbage. In nineteen seventy-four, the biologist Roger Knutson reported in the journal Science that its flower spike stays fifteen to thirty-five degrees Celsius warmer than the air around it, even when the air drops to minus fifteen. For at least fourteen days, it uses oxygen about as fast as a warm-blooded animal of the same size. How does a plant run a furnace? Researchers studying a closely related Asian skunk cabbage found that the cells around its stamens make two mitochondrial bypasses at once. One is an alternative oxidase, which hands electrons straight to oxygen without pumping protons. The other is an uncoupling protein, which lets protons slip back across the inner membrane. Either way, less of the energy becomes A T P and more becomes heat, enough to melt the snow around the flower.

Second, remember how this lesson opened, with cyanide jamming Complex four. Nobody told Madagascar's golden bamboo lemur. In nineteen eighty-nine, Kenneth Glander, Patricia Wright and their colleagues measured the growing tips of the bamboo these small primates eat. Every hundred grams of fresh tips held fifteen milligrams of cyanide. Each lemur ate about five hundred grams of bamboo a day, which the researchers worked out to be about twelve times the lethal dose of cyanide, every single day. The lemurs showed no sign of poisoning. Later urine tests suggest they get rid of some of it, but exactly how they cope with that much is still not worked out.

Third, reactive oxygen species. Exercise raises them in muscle, and they have a bad reputation, so taking antioxidant vitamins while you train sounds sensible. In two thousand nine, Michael Ristow and his colleagues tested that idea in thirty-nine healthy young men on a four-week exercise program, with about half of them taking vitamins C and E every day. The men who trained without the vitamins became more sensitive to insulin, and their muscles turned up the genes for their own antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase. The men on the vitamins did not show those changes. The authors read this as the vitamins blunting a small puff of reactive oxygen species that exercise normally sends as a signal. But a later Danish trial, run for twelve weeks, found that insulin sensitivity improved just as much with or without the vitamins. So treat it as a fascinating, unsettled clue, not as a rule about vitamins.

So there you have it: a flower that turns its chain's energy into heat to melt the snow, a lemur that lives on cyanide-rich bamboo, and muscles that may use a puff of oxidants as a message. Three very different lives, all running on the chain you just learned.
